items.title: Jack DeJohnette interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 7, 2025
items.q: And I had the opportunity to play with him with John Coltrane in Chicago at the Plugged Nickel with Alice and Jimmy and Pharoah Sanders.

ctx.x: I had the fortunate circumstance of right next door to this office I’m sitting I had Rashied Ali and Henry Grimes here and that was just wonderful to listen to them talk about music and Rashied said something about, you know you’re talking about free jazz and many people think that it sounds angry. And he straightened me out on that, he just said it was the times we were in, it was a reflection of the times, and he did talk about the experiences he had in the military with segregation and so forth, and it was…

Yeah. Well you know I know Rashied and he’s very interesting. He’s a very musical drummer actually. And he found another way of playing, which was a multi — like a sound and a vibration that John Coltrane could play. I mean a lot of people, you know, not only he said it but Rashied used to play a lot of time. In fact I sat in on piano with him at his club Green Street. But he always carried a flute with him. So he’s very musical. But he discovered a way to play the drums in such a way that was very concentrated.…

And that was amazing. I learned a lot from Rashied just playing next to him. Because I was young and cocky and there I saw Rashied in terms of stamina and focus and concentration you know. I would play full out and then I’d get tired and stop and he’d be playing, he’d still be going. And I realized oh, he figured out a way to create the dynamics with a concentrated effort.

items.title: Jack DeJohnette — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: went up to the bandstand and I followed him up and I subsequently played three tunes with him.

ctx.x: Was Pat Patrick already in Sun Ra's band at this point too?

Yeah, he was playing on and off with Sun Ra. Pat would play when Sun Ra needed baritone or an alto or something because Pat played all the horns . . . Pat also helped me when I came to New York, but we'll talk about that later . . . I had a trio and I started working and getting gigs as a drummer. This was maybe the late 50s going into the 60s. I was working with some blues bands and I actually had a gig where I had hired Eddie Harris, he had Exodus To Jazz was popular then. I hired Eddie as a special guest for…
That was with the quartet? Elvin, McCoy, and Jimmy? Or Reggie?
